source: Araya (2025) Do Chains-of-Thoughts of LLMs suffer from hallucinations, cognitive biases, or phobias in Bayesian reasoning?
finding: One Bayes item (cat-lies, card-in-book puzzle) given to Gemini Flash 2.0, o3-mini and DeepSeek R1 in Feb 2025. With the plain prompt none used natural frequencies. Adding 'consider Gigerenzer natural frequencies' got partial, shallow use.
numbers: Plain prompt: Gemini run twice (255 words correct, 389 words wrong); o3-mini 2039 words, wrong; R1 2786 words, correct via Bayes formula. With the frequency hint Gemini was correct but only changed the language in 90% and kept percentages; o3-mini did a 1000-case count in a second pass. N = one item, one or two runs per model.
limits: Single item, no accuracy rate, no control for the hint's extra tokens, qualitative reading by one author. Not a test of whether frequency wording helps.
agent_relevance: Reasoning models default to symbolic Bayes and may ignore a frequency suggestion. A restatement step should be done by code or by a fixed rewrite, not requested as a style hint.

source: Huang, Zhang, Kwak, An (2026) CogBias: Measuring and Mitigating Cognitive Bias in LLMs
finding: Read the full text. Its related-work line says natural frequency formats reduce base-rate neglect in humans and LLMs, citing Dasgupta 2022. CogBias itself runs no frequency-format manipulation. Its prompt-level debiasing reduced Response biases but backfired for Judgment biases (the family with Bayes items).
numbers: Three LLMs; activation steering cut bias score 26-32%; prompt-level debiasing 'backfires for Judgment biases'.
quote: natural frequency formats reduce base-rate neglect in both humans (Gigerenzer & Hoffrage, 1995) and LLMs (Dasgupta et al., 2022)
limits: A secondary statement, not a measurement. Per-item debiasing numbers were not extracted.
agent_relevance: Do not rely on the LLM-frequency-format claim; it has no measurement behind it here. Generic debias prompts can make judgement items worse.

source: Lampinen, Dasgupta et al. (2022/2024) Language models show human-like content effects on reasoning tasks
finding: Read the full text and searched it for frequency, base rate, Bayes. Tasks are natural language inference, syllogisms and the Wason selection task, comparing abstract vs believable content. There is no natural-frequency or Bayes-format test.
numbers: No frequency-format numbers exist in the paper. The only Bayes hit is a reference title (Cohen et al., Beliefs and Bayesian reasoning).
limits: Content effects are a different manipulation (semantic belief), not number format.
agent_relevance: The Dasgupta-to-frequency chain (K11) is a mis-citation. Close the chain as false; the LLM frequency-format question stays unmeasured.

source: Menon, Zemel, Vondrick (2024) Whiteboard-of-Thought: Thinking Step-by-Step Across Modalities
finding: GPT-4o writes matplotlib/turtle code, the code is run, and the rendered image is fed back. On navigation over different tile geometries the picture beats text CoT where text coordinates are awkward and loses on the square grid.
limits: One model (GPT-4o, temperature 0). Task is Yamada et al. navigation. The picture is code-built, not freehand. Tokens not matched. Not a 2026 reasoning model.
agent_relevance: Choose a render when the text form has no easy coordinate system (hexagon 8 to 61); keep text when a coordinate grid is natural (square 98 vs 50). Candidate task feature: does the text form map to coordinates the model has seen often.

source: Menon et al. (2024) Whiteboard-of-Thought, ASCII recognition and error analysis
finding: On BIG-Bench ASCII word recognition, text alone scored 0% on several 'visual' ASCII types while WoT reached 92.1% on the best. For MNIST ASCII the model gets 80.8% on real MNIST images, so most WoT errors come from poor perception, not from the drawing code.
numbers: Table 2 rows (column labels not recovered from the PDF text): Direct 0.0/0.0/100.0/50.0/0.0; CoT 0.0/0.0/100.0/62.5/0.0; WoT 92.1/78.0/42.1/89.6/11.8. Perception upper bound 80.8% on actual MNIST images.
limits: Column names were lost in text extraction, so only the pattern (text fails, image wins, except one column where text is 100 and WoT 42.1) is safe to quote.
agent_relevance: A render can also lose; the agent needs a check that the render came out as intended. Perception, not drawing, is the remaining error source.

source: Li et al. (2025) Imagine while Reasoning in Space: Multimodal Visualization-of-Thought (MVoT)
finding: Text CoT that writes the grid state fails mainly because the written state is wrong. On FrozenLake, 90.80% of CoT errors came from inaccurate coordinates of holes, and CoT accuracy fell with grid size.
numbers: CoT on FrozenLake: 0.9401 (3x3) to 0.3911 (6x6). MVoT (fine-tuned Anole-7B): Maze 92.95%, MiniBehavior 95.14%, FrozenLake 85.60%; CoT over 95% on Maze and MiniBehavior but below Direct on FrozenLake. GPT-4o zero-shot worse than Direct with and without CoT.
limits: MVoT is fine-tuned on task data (7B model), so not a prompt-only test. Not token-matched. GPT-4o version 2024-07-01.
agent_relevance: Supports K04: the written state is the weak point. A code-checked state list targets exactly the 90.8% error source. Image gains here come with training, so do not expect them in a prompt-only agent.

source: Hu et al. (2024) Visual Sketchpad, Appendix E costs
finding: The cost table lists tokens per sample for Sketchpad runs with GPT-4o. No matched-token baseline is reported anywhere in the paper.
numbers: Tokens per sample: Math Parity 2994, Math Convexity 2211, Graph Connectivity 2819, Graph Isomorphism 3143, V*Bench 26647, MMVP 11870, BLINK 11508-16988. Cost $0.011-0.016 per sample on math and graph tasks, $0.133 on V*Bench.
limits: Cost only; the plain-CoT arm's token count is not given, so net value per token cannot be computed.
agent_relevance: Confirms gap 1 stays open for Sketchpad: its gains cost thousands of tokens and no equal-token control exists.

source: Aytes, Baek, Hwang (2025) Sketch-of-Thought: Efficient LLM Reasoning with Adaptive Cognitive-Inspired Sketching
finding: Writing the reasoning as terse structured sketches (chunked symbols, concept chains, expert lexicons) keeps accuracy at about a quarter of the CoT tokens, so a compact written form is not a loss. A small router (DistilBERT, 14,200 machine-labelled examples) picks one of three forms per question.
numbers: Up to 84% token cut (abstract); average over 74% with accuracy within 1%. GPT-4o 84.55% vs CoT 84.64 (-0.09). Qwen-2.5-32B 82.30 vs CoT 82.24. Commonsense 92.00% at 34 tokens vs 91.48% at 177 tokens under CoT. With self-consistency: 176 vs 680 tokens, 81.90 vs 81.86.
limits: Non-reasoning models (GPT-4o, Sonnet 3.5, Qwen). Router trained once on pooled training splits, so its cost is amortised, not paid per item; it needs labelled data per task family. Gains are token efficiency, not accuracy.
agent_relevance: Equal-token comparisons are feasible: give plain CoT the same capped budget. A fixed router trained once answers part of gap 7 (selection cost not paid per item), but a pilot-on-a-few-items scheme was not tested.

source: Xu, Xie, Zhao, He (2025) Chain of Draft: Thinking Faster by Writing Less
finding: Capping each reasoning step at about five words cuts output about 80% on GSM8K with a small accuracy loss, and on some tasks gains over CoT.
numbers: GSM8K: GPT-4o CoT 95.4%, CoD 91.1%; Claude 3.5 Sonnet CoT 95.8%, CoD 91.4%; standard 53.3% and 64.6%; CoD about 40 tokens vs about 200. Sports: GPT-4o CoT 95.9, CoD 98.3; Claude CoT 93.2, CoD 97.3. Dates: GPT-4o CoT 90.2, CoD 88.1; Claude CoT 87.0, CoD 89.7.
limits: Few-shot with hand-written drafts; zero-shot drafting is weaker (authors note). Non-reasoning models. Table columns were partly garbled in extraction.
agent_relevance: Gives a token-capped baseline: any representation claim should beat a terse draft CoT at the same length, not only verbose CoT.

source: Cao and Liu (2026, ICLR) TableMaster: A Recipe to Advance Table Understanding with Language Models
finding: Plain text reasoning on tables breaks when arithmetic is needed; code reasoning on a messy table breaks worse; normalising structure first and mixing text-guided code is best. Code-built representation helps only after the input is cleaned.
numbers: Calculation-needed questions: textual reasoning falls 20.1% vs 7.6% for enhanced symbolic. On a noisy table format, symbolic falls 31.8% vs textual 20.5%. Text-guided symbolic reasoning reaches 59.1% on calculation-needed questions. WikiTQ 78.13% with GPT-4o-mini, +3.51/+13.40/+12.39 over best baselines for gpt-3.5-turbo / gpt-4o-mini / Llama-3.1-70B.
limits: Pipeline of many steps (extraction, verbalisation, normalisation); gains not attributed to form alone. Small models. No token accounting.
agent_relevance: Supports K05 and sets a boundary: a code-built form fails if built from a noisy raw input. Normalise and verify the state before computing on it.

source: Tam et al. (2024) Let Me Speak Freely? Impact of Format Restrictions on LLM Performance
finding: Forcing the answer into JSON hurts reasoning tasks with several models; stricter constraints hurt more; putting the answer key before the reason key kills the reasoning. Schema-constrained decoding with reason first is close to free text.
numbers: gpt-4o-mini, mean of 9 prompts (NL / format-restricting instructions / JSON-mode / JSON-schema): GSM8K 94.57 / 87.17 / 86.95 / 91.71; Shuffled Objects 82.85 / 81.46 / 76.43 / 81.77; Last Letter 83.11 / 84.73 / 76.00 / 86.07. GPT-3.5 JSON-mode: 100% of responses put answer before reason. LLaMA-3-8B parse error 0.148% yet 38.15% accuracy gap on Last Letter.
limits: Models: gpt-3.5, claude-3-haiku, gemini-1.5-flash, gpt-4o-mini, LLaMA-3-8B, Gemma-2-9B. No reasoning models. Standard deviations across prompts up to about 10 points.
agent_relevance: Format spread still exists in 2024 small and mid models. Put reasoning fields before answer fields; do not constrain the thinking channel. Measure on our own model before trusting any spread.

source: Sclar et al. (2024, ICLR) Quantifying Language Models' Sensitivity to Spurious Features in Prompt Design
finding: Meaning-preserving formatting changes (separators, casing, spacing) move accuracy by up to 76 points on LLaMA-2-13B. Sensitivity is not removed by larger models, more few-shot examples or instruction tuning.
numbers: Up to 76 accuracy points (LLaMA-2-13B); Llama-2-70B spread shown in Fig. 11; GPT-3.5 also sensitive.
quote: sensitivity ... is not eliminated by adding few-shot examples, increasing model size, or instruction tuning
limits: Surface formatting, not representation choice. Only open and 2023 models and GPT-3.5; no reasoning models.
agent_relevance: This contradicts the K06 note that spread shrinks for the strongest models: this source says it does not shrink with size. Still unmeasured for 2025-2026 reasoning models, so run a small format-noise test on our model.

source: Liu et al. (2024) Lost in the Middle: How Language Models Use Long Contexts
finding: Closest LLM analogue of Larkin and Simon locality: where the needed fact sits matters. Accuracy is highest when the relevant document is first or last in a 20-document context and falls in the middle.
numbers: GPT-3.5-Turbo 20-document QA: worst case (answer mid-context) falls more than 20 points from best and below its closed-book 56.1%; oracle 88.3%; Claude-1.3 closed-book 48.3%, oracle 76.1%.
limits: Retrieval QA, not diagrammatic inference; 2023 models. Position effect, not adjacent vs scattered inference steps.
agent_relevance: Put the facts a step needs next to the step (ledger line beside the constraint). This is an indirect test; a direct adjacent-vs-scattered test on a reasoning model is still missing.

source: Jiang, Ilievski, Ma, Sourati (2023) BRAINTEASER: Lateral Thinking Puzzles for LLMs
finding: Insight-type puzzles: strong models are far from human level. The paper tests rephrasing (semantic reconstruction) and a context swap that keeps the misleading premise; it does not test stating the hidden constraint.
numbers: ChatGPT about 53% (sentence puzzles) and 63% (word puzzles) vs human 92% and random 25%. Human check: 100% of semantic and 97% of context reconstructions marked consistent with the original.
limits: 2023 models. No condition that reveals the constraint, so it cannot answer gap 8.
agent_relevance: Our portfolio has this benchmark; an arm 'constraint stated' vs plain would be a first test. No transfer of Macchi is shown to date.

source: Deng, Zhang, Chen, Gu (2024) Rephrase and Respond: Let LLMs Ask Better Questions for Themselves
finding: Having GPT-4 rewrite the question before answering raised zero-shot accuracy, mostly where the original wording was poor. The baseline is direct zero-shot, not CoT, and gains shrink where the baseline is already high.
numbers: GPT-4 averages over 10 tasks: original 64.95, RaR variant 89.77. Last-letter (2 words) 52.05 to 99.09; (4 words) 21.36 to 86.82; coin flip 74.55 to 99.09; Age 98.44 to 100; CSQA 84.09 to 85.45. GPT-3.5 and Vicuna gain less and slightly lose on Sports.
limits: Baseline has no CoT; the CoT comparison is limited to a combined prompt and a flawed-example test. 2023 GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Answers gap 9 in part: rewriting gains are large against a weak baseline and small against a strong one. Always include a plain CoT arm and a terse-CoT arm.

source: Franzen, Disselhoff, Hartmann (2025) Product of Experts with LLMs: Boosting Performance on ARC Is a Matter of Perspective
finding: Same ARC task shown under rotations, transposes and colour permutations; candidate answers are scored by how likely they are under every view. Format is one token per cell with no extra delimiters.
numbers: 71.6% (286.5 of 400 tasks) on the public evaluation set with an open 8B model; their table lists o3 58.5, TTT 60.2, average human 82.8.
limits: Fine-tuned model with test-time training and DFS sampling, so not a prompt-only result. It changes view, not detail level, so does not settle gap 5.
agent_relevance: Re-viewing the same grid under a transform and checking agreement is a cheap verification idea. It does not tell us which object-list detail level is best.
